newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan warlord said to lose military headquarters.
newsitem.headline: Afghan warlord said to lose military headquarters.

text.p: The northern Afghan town of Shibarghan, the military headquarters of opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum, fell to his opponents on Saturday amid a revolt in his small air force, his opponents said.

Sources in the dominant Taleban Islamic movement, quoted by a Pakistan-based private Afghan news service, said the town, capital of Jozjan province, was captured by anti-Dostum forces led by Taleban leader Abdul Razzaq, governor of the western province of Herat.

There was no immediate independent confirmation of the report, which came hours after three jet fighters of Dostum's air force defected to his opponents, and only a day after Western reporters drove to the town from the main northern town of Mazar-i-Sharif to find it calm.
The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) agency also said defectors later flew another jet to Kabul and two helicopters to Maimana.

Panic swept Mazar-i-Sharif, a Dostum stronghold and capital of Balkh province, on Saturday afternoon after reports that Shibarghan, 130 km (80 miles) west of there, had fallen, Reuters correspondent Alistair Lyon reported from there.
But there was no immediate confirmation of the reports there and no word on Dostum's whereabouts.
Shopkeepers in Mazar-i-Sharif pulled down their shutters, soldiers ran away in tanks and security men roughed up foreign cameramen, witnesses said. Some soldiers were stealing cars.
Streets emptied in a flash as people raced to get home, and witnesses said some were trying to flee the city northwards towards the Uzbek border.

Earlier, a defecting officer of Dostum's air force, Major General Yussef Shah, told reporters in Kabul that he made the 35-minute flight in his L39 Albatross trainer from Shibarghan airport to the capital because he feared that Dostum was trying to split Afghanistan. .
Two Soviet-built Su-22 fighter bombers were earlier flown from Shibarghan to Maimana, capital of Faryab province, he said.

"We feared that Dostum was trying to dismantle Afghanistan. More planes are expected to come over," Yussef, clean-shaven and wearing combat fatigues, told reporters gathered in the Kabul office of the head of the Taleban air force.
Maimana is held by Dostum's former foreign minister and deputy, General Abdul Malik, who launched a revolt against Dostum on Monday.
"One of the pilots was Colonel General Hafeez, the head of (Dostum's) air force. They bombed Shibarghan air base on their way out," said Yussef.
It was not possible to confirm the bombings or the defections to Maimana.
Yussef said Saturday's defections meant that Dostum had lost more than a quarter of his air force.
"Dostum had four Su-22s, three MiG-21s, and four L39s before today, now he has lost three of them," he said.
Yussef said the Taleban and their new ally, General Malik, faced Dostum's forces on a front line some 15 km (nine miles) from Shibarghan.
He said that Dostum's forces still held the town of Sar-i-Pul, but that the Taleban forces were within two km (1-1/4 miles) of the town.
The opposition alliance led by Dostum, who has led the fight against the purist Islamic Taleban, was thrown into disarray by Malik's revolt on Monday.
The revolt broke an 18-month deadlock on the front line in Badghis province.
The Taleban, who seized Kabul last September and control most of Afghanistan, now command all of Badghis and its eastern neighbour Faryab and are making inroads into Sar-i-pul province.
